title: Practical applications of photon-counting CT in oncology: an organ-based pictorial review.
abstract: Spectral computed tomography (CT) has become an important extension of contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) in oncologic imaging by providing material-specific information beyond conventional morphologic assessment. Dual-energy CT (DECT), implemented on energy-integrating detector CT (EID-CT) platforms, has demonstrated the value of low-keV virtual monoenergetic imaging (VMI), iodine mapping, and material decomposition for improving tumor conspicuity, delineating local extent, and supporting tissue characterization. However, broader clinical adoption of EID-CT-based DECT has been limited by increased low-keV image noise and workflow complexity. Photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) addresses these limitations by offering improved energy resolution, reduced electronic noise, and routine acquisition of multi-energy data without dedicated dual-energy protocols. In particular, low-keV VMI around 40 keV can be generated with clinically acceptable noise, enabling consistent enhancement-based assessment in daily practice. Iodine-based reconstructions further complement morphologic evaluation by visualizing viable tumor enhancement and enabling quantitative analysis. This organ-based pictorial review summarizes practical applications of PCD-CT-based spectral imaging in oncology. Across organ systems, spectral CT may provide complementary problem-solving information by improving lesion detection, tumor extent delineation, and diagnostic confidence, particularly when conventional CT findings are equivocal, or MRI is unavailable, contraindicated, or limited. Emerging quantitative parameters, including electron density, effective atomic number, and advanced material decomposition, may further expand oncologic CT applications, although outcome-driven validation remains limited. Together, these features position PCD-CT as a practical spectral imaging platform for routine oncologic CT. KEY POINTS: Question How can PCD-CT address low-keV image noise and workflow barriers that have limited routine DECT-based spectral imaging in oncologic CT practice? Findings PCD-CT enables low-keV VMI and iodine-based reconstructions that may improve lesion conspicuity, tumor-extent assessment, and problem-solving across organ-specific oncologic workflows. Critical relevance statement This review clarifies practical, evidence-aware uses of PCD-CT spectral reconstructions in oncology, highlighting low-keV VMI as an adjunct, selective iodine-map problem-solving, and investigational quantitative parameters.

title: The diagnostic value of high-resolution 3D T2-weighted MRI in preoperative evaluation and classification of Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich syndrome: a prospective study.
abstract: Objective Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich syndrome (HWWS) is a rare female reproductive tract malformation. Accurate preoperative diagnosis and classification are vital for surgical planning. This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic value of high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) T2-weighted MRI in the preoperative assessment and classification of HWWS. Materials and methods The study prospectively enrolled 84 patients clinically diagnosed with HWWS between May 2020 and January 2025. Seventy patients underwent pelvic MRI examinations, including high-resolution 3D T2 sequences (1 mm slice thickness) and conventional T2 TSE sequences, supplemented by large-field-of-view (FOV) T2 coronal imaging for urinary system evaluation and full-spine X-ray examinations for skeletal assessment. Two experienced radiologists independently evaluated the imaging features in a blinded manner, focusing on uterine morphology, obstruction sites, presence of communications, and related anomalies and complications. Consistency analysis was performed between imaging findings and surgical results in 52 surgical patients. Results Uterine morphology included: didelphys (54/70, 77.1%), complete septate (14/70, 20%), and bicornuate uterus (2/70, 2.9%). Among 52 surgical patients, 31 (59.6%) had vaginal-level obstruction with 18 (34.6%) Type I, 11 (21.2%) Type II, and 2 (3.8%) Type III, and 21 (40.4%) had cervical-level obstruction (Type IV and mixed). 3D T2 sequences identified 7 (63.6%) vaginal septum fistulas, outperforming TSE sequences, which detected none (0%) (p = 0.005). Associated findings were ipsilateral renal agenesis (98.6%), ovarian endometriosis (22.9%), hematosalpinx (22.9%), and spinal abnormalities (scoliosis (25.7%), mild scoliosis (41.4%). Conclusion High-resolution 3D T2 MRI is superior to conventional T2 TSE sequences in the preoperative evaluation of HWWS, especially for identifying communications and precisely locating obstruction sites. Key points Question Accurate preoperative structural assessment and classification of HWWS are clinically essential, yet conventional MRI has limitations in identifying fine anatomical structures and small communications. Findings High-resolution 3D T2 MRI outperforms conventional T2 TSE in identifying vaginal and cervical communications and precisely localizing obstruction sites in preoperative evaluation of HWWS. Critical relevance statement This study supports routine inclusion of 3D sequences in HWWS imaging protocols. Combined with renal and spinal assessment, it provides a comprehensive preoperative evaluation that enhances surgical planning precision and optimizes patient management strategies.

title: Contralateral-controlled thigh muscle biomarkers on CT angiography for prediction of 1-year restenosis after endovascular therapy for unilateral peripheral artery disease.
abstract: Objective To develop and internally validate a model using contralateral-controlled thigh muscle biomarkers, measured on routine computed tomography angiography (CTA), to predict clinically driven, DSA-confirmed 1-year restenosis after endovascular therapy for unilateral peripheral artery disease (PAD). Materials and methods In this retrospective cohort study, 378 patients with unilateral PAD undergoing endovascular therapy and having baseline and 1-year follow-up CTA were included. Mid-thigh skeletal muscle cross-sectional area and whole-thigh muscle volume were quantified bilaterally with semi-automated software. Contralateral-controlled biomarkers (affected minus contralateral) were derived to isolate limb-specific ischemic effects. The primary endpoint was clinically driven 1-year restenosis (≥ 50%) confirmed by DSA. Results Among 378 patients, 162 (43%) developed restenosis at a median follow-up of 12.5 months. Contralateral-controlled muscle asymmetry was independently associated with restenosis after adjustment for lesion length, baseline stenosis degree, Fontaine stage, disease duration, and TASC II classification (OR 1.43, 95% CI: 1.08-1.89, p = 0.01). Adding muscle asymmetry to a severity-only model improved discrimination from AUC 0.76 to 0.79 (DeLong p = 0.04). A baseline predictive model combining lesion length and muscle asymmetry achieved AUC 0.74; a full explanatory model incorporating longitudinal muscle changes reached AUC 0.88, with the greatest net benefit on decision curve analysis. Conclusion Thigh muscle biomarkers, acquired opportunistically from routine CTA scans, improved the prediction of 1-year restenosis after endovascular therapy and may support targeted surveillance in patients with unilateral PAD. Key points Question Can contralateral-controlled thigh muscle biomarkers on routine CT angiography improve the prediction of 1-year restenosis after endovascular therapy for unilateral peripheral artery disease? Findings In 378 PAD patients, baseline contralateral thigh muscle asymmetry independently predicted clinically driven, DSA-confirmed restenosis and improved AUC from 0.76 to 0.79. Critical relevance statement Opportunistic contralateral-controlled thigh muscle analysis on routine CT angiography provides a no-cost imaging biomarker that refines post-endovascular restenosis risk stratification, supporting targeted angiographic surveillance and advancing personalized vascular imaging practice in peripheral artery disease.

title: Myocardial work in light-chain and transthyretin-related amyloidosis with preserved ejection fraction: a cardiovascular magnetic resonance study.
abstract: Objectives To investigate pressure-volume loop (PV-loop) changes by cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging in cardiac amyloidosis (CA) patients with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), and to assess PV-loop parameters' potential as subtype differential diagnostic markers. Materials and methods Between May 2017 and September 2023, 100 consecutive confirmed CA patients (14 transthyretin-related [ATTR-CA] and 86 light-chain [AL-CA]) and 40 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) were prospectively enrolled. PV-loop parameters were derived from CMR cine images and brachial blood pressure. Clinical and CMR parameters were compared between CA patients and HCs, as well as between CA subtypes. The correlations between PV-loop parameters and clinical and imaging parameters were assessed. Furthermore, the differential diagnostic performance of these PV-loop parameters was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). Bootstrapping was performed 2000 times for internal validation. Results Compared to HCs, CA patients showed significantly lower stroke work index, potential energy index (PEI), and work efficiency (all p < 0.001). AL-CA patients had higher N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels (2358.00 [IQR: 903.25, 5559.00] vs 810.00 [IQR: 269.00, 1136.01] pg/mL, p = 0.002) and lower PEI (0.13 [IQR: 0.07, 0.15] vs 0.15 [IQR: 0.13, 0.19] J/m², p = 0.025) than ATTR-CA patients. NT-proBNP (β = -1.94, OR = 0.14, 95% CI: 0.03-0.64, p = 0.016) and PEI (β = 0.20, OR = 1.23, 95% CI: 1.07-1.44, p = 0.007) were independent predictors for AL-CA vs ATTR-CA differentiation, and combining these two parameters enhanced the diagnostic performance (bootstrapping AUC 0.847). Conclusion By providing pathophysiological insights into the distinctions between AL-CA and ATTR-CA, PV-loop parameters have the potential to serve as a complementary, contrast-free approach for differential diagnosis. Key points Question PV-loop changes by CMR in CA patients with preserved LVEF remain unknown. Findings Light-chain CA patients with preserved LVEF had higher NT-proBNP levels and lower PEI than transthyretin-related CA patients. Critical relevance statement The CMR-derived PV-loop parameters revealed pathophysiological differences between the two subtypes of CA, suggesting potential differential diagnostic value.

title: Optimizing AI-assisted decision-making in mammography screening: focusing on uncertainties.
abstract: Objective To evaluate an AI-based decision-support system for mammography interpretation, assessing its impact on diagnostic performance. Materials and methods This retrospective study analyzed 130,838 mammograms from 35,709 patients with confirmed follow-up outcomes across multiple centers, using the Digital Database for Screening Mammography (DDSM) for external validation. Representing one of the largest datasets from the Middle East, it evaluates model generalizability in underrepresented populations. An AI super-model incorporated separate UNet-based networks for lesion segmentation, a high-resolution model (4096) for calcifications, a multi-resolution ensemble (4096, 2048, 1024) for macro-scale lesions, and a risk-assessment model for malignancy prediction. Radiologists interpreted images under five scenarios: unaided, AI-assisted, AI as the final decision-maker in uncertain cases, union of radiologist and AI decisions in uncertain cases, and standalone AI. Results AI assistance significantly enhanced performance across all scenarios. Based on aggregated reader performance, AUC improved from 83.04% (95% CI: 79.8-86.3) unaided to 88.40% (95% CI: 85.6-91.2) in the union scenario (p < 0.001). Sensitivity increased from 54.8% (95% CI: 48.6-61.0) to 83.9% (95% CI: 79.3-88.4) (p < 0.001), and specificity rose from 83.6% (95% CI: 82.0-85.3) to 91.1% (95% CI: 89.8-92.4) (p < 0.001). Multi-resolution segmentation effectively detected calcifications and challenging lesions. DDSM validation confirmed model robustness. AI showed particular promise in aiding less-experienced radiologists in underserved areas to improve early cancer detection. Conclusions AI in mammography interpretation improves diagnostic accuracy and reduces uncertainty, supporting early breast cancer detection and optimized screening workflows. Key points Question Can an AI-based decision-support system improve the accuracy of mammography interpretation, reduce diagnostic uncertainty, and support less-experienced radiologists? Findings In this retrospective multicenter study, AI-assisted mammography improved sensitivity and specificity, increased cancer detection, and reduced recalls and false positives. Critical relevance statement AI integration in mammography enhances diagnostic accuracy, reduces unnecessary recalls, and supports more confident and efficient clinical decision-making, particularly by improving the performance of less-experienced radiologists in underserved and resource-limited settings where expert interpretation may be limited.

title: Colour maps for representation of quantitative metrics in radiology: meaningful or misleading?
abstract: The increased utility of quantitative metrics in medical imaging has prompted the use of colour representation of the data. Colour schemes for image display can highlight pathology and distinguish normal anatomy, thus potentially aiding image interpretation. Adding colour schemes to images may serve the sole purpose of visualising an abnormality or may seek to represent and meaningfully convey a quantitative metric. An early use of colour representation is exemplified by colour Doppler in ultrasound (US), where a two-sided linear scale is commonly applied. More recently, many schemes have arisen, ranging from a single colour to depict a segmented region to a range of colours that embrace the entire colour spectrum. These may be applied as continuous or discrete palettes, depending on the software vendor or even on individual user settings. The lack of standardisation of colour schemes across the medical community, especially in medical imaging, risks misinterpretation of quantitative data and potential unintended negative clinical consequences. The purpose of this article is to review the colour schemes used for quantitative imaging across US, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography (PET), the way in which they are applied, the clinical applications where their use is desirable for enhanced interpretation, and the pitfalls where standardisation is lacking in a variety of clinical applications. Finally, we discuss some solutions that could be employed to enable standardisation and augment the use of colour in image interpretation. KEY POINTS: Question Colour schemes in medical imaging can highlight pathology, but standardisation is lacking for most imaging modalities, thus risking misinterpretation of quantitative data. Findings For T1, T2, and T2* maps and their inverses, colour map recommendations have recently been proposed, but are mostly lacking for other quantitative data. Critical relevance statement Standardised colour maps can enhance data analyses across scanners and institutions, which is important for multicentre studies and handling big data. Furthermore, standardised and harmonised colour maps could improve lesion conspicuity, cross-platform comparability, and longitudinal reliability.

title: Impact of deep learning image reconstruction on CT radiomics reproducibility in patients with pulmonary nodules.
abstract: Objective Ensuring CT feature reproducibility across imaging protocols and reconstruction algorithms is essential for the generalizability of radiomics applications. This study aimed to evaluate the reproducibility of CT radiomic features in pulmonary nodules using deep learning image reconstruction (DLIR) compared with conventional reconstruction techniques under different radiation doses. Materials and methods We included 94 patients between March and June 2023. Standard- and low-dose CT images were scanned to assess the impact of dose reduction on feature reproducibility. DLIR strengths at low (DLIR-L), medium (DLIR-M), and high (DLIR-H), representing progressive levels of noise suppression, were compared against filtered back projection (FBP) and adaptive statistical iterative reconstruction-V at 50% strength (ASIR-V-50%) reconstructions. 2264 features were extracted from pulmonary nodules. The concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) and the coefficient of variation (CV) were used to evaluate inter-dose reproducibility, inter-reconstruction reproducibility, and feature variability. Results The mean CCC for inter-dose reproducibility using DLIR-H, ASIR-V-50%, and FBP was 0.934 ± 0.104, 0.922 ± 0.128, and 0.922 ± 0.113, respectively (p = 0.055), with 29.8%, 27.9%, and 20.2% of features showing near-perfect agreement. In low-dose CT, DLIR-L achieved the highest inter-reconstruction reproducibility against ASIR-V-50% (0.950 ± 0.094), with 39.4% of features showing near-perfect agreement. The overall CV across reconstructions was 9.87 ± 20.32%, with 74.0% of features highly stable. Part-solid nodules showed the lowest variability (7.17 ± 13.48%, p < 0.001). Reproducibility improved significantly with increasing nodule size (p < 0.001). Conclusion DLIR improves the radiomic feature reproducibility in pulmonary nodules, making it particularly suitable for low-dose CT protocols. However, the robustness tends to decrease with higher DLIR strengths. Nodule characteristics significantly influence variability. Key points Question The impact of DLIR on radiomic feature reproducibility across radiation doses and reconstruction methods in pulmonary nodules remains unknown. Findings DLIR-H demonstrated high inter-dose reproducibility, while DLIR-L achieved the highest inter-reconstruction reproducibility; feature variability decreased significantly with increasing nodule size, with 21 robust features identified. Critical relevance statementThis study critically assesses reconstruction-related instability in CT radiomics and identifies DLIR settings and nodule characteristics that influence feature robustness, supporting protocol optimization and more reliable quantitative pulmonary nodule assessment in clinical radiology.

title: Imaging in localized intrahepatic bile duct dilatation: a pictorial review of diagnostic and differential approaches.
abstract: Localized intrahepatic bile duct dilatation (LIBD) is a prevalent radiological finding characterized by a variety of etiologies, including congenital anomalies, inflammatory conditions, hepatolithiasis, and neoplastic lesions. Accurate differential diagnosis of diseases associated with LIBD is crucial for formulating appropriate treatment strategies and improving patient prognosis. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the definitions, etiologies, clinical symptoms, and key imaging features of common diseases associated with LIBD. Furthermore, it proposes a structured approach for differential diagnosis. By integrating imaging findings with clinical and laboratory data, this approach aims to improve diagnostic accuracy and assist radiologists in making optimal clinical decisions. KEY POINTS: Question LIBD has diverse etiologies and overlapping imaging patterns, but a practical, standardized radiological framework for differential diagnosis remains lacking. Findings This pictorial review summarizes characteristic CT/MRI findings of common LIBD-associated diseases and establishes a stepwise diagnostic approach integrating obstruction points, morphology, and clinical information. Critical Relevance Statement By combining specific imaging patterns with clinical context, this review provides a practical differential diagnostic framework that may improve diagnostic confidence, guide further evaluation, and facilitate earlier detection of malignant transformation in LIBD.

title: Ultrasonography in disaster medicine: a narrative review.
abstract: This narrative review aimed to critically appraise the diagnostic accuracy, clinical impact, and operational feasibility of ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography (POCUS) across the four domains of disaster medicine. A literature search was conducted following the SANRA and PRISMA-trAIce guidelines. Records were identified through an AI-assisted literature-discovery tool (the Undermind Deep-Search platform, interrogating the Semantic Scholar corpus) run on 15 June 2025, rather than through an independent structured multi-database search. Candidate references were screened manually against pre-specified eligibility criteria by a single reviewer, with the search parameters independently verified by the senior author. Of 71 records identified, 63 met the inclusion criteria. The included studies comprised 32 original studies, 10 systematic or scoping reviews, 20 narrative or operational papers, and one guideline. In CBRN scenarios, lung ultrasound demonstrated sensitivities of 90-97% for COVID-19 pneumonia versus 60-69% for chest radiography while minimizing healthcare worker exposure. For blast and ballistic injuries, FAST showed a pooled sensitivity of 92.1% (95% CI: 87.8-95.6) and specificity of 98.7% (95% CI: 96.0-99.9) for intra-abdominal hemorrhage. In natural disasters, ultrasound altered management in up to 44% of patients. Post-disaster applications included vascular access, tube confirmation, and complication monitoring. Ultraportable POCUS demonstrates diagnostic utility and operational feasibility across multiple disaster domains. However, evidence quality varies significantly, and standardized protocols remain lacking. Prospective studies linking ultrasound deployment to improved patient outcomes are needed. KEY POINTS: Question When disasters disable conventional imaging, how does ultraportable point-of-care ultrasonography perform for diagnosis, triage, and procedural guidance across the four domains of disaster medicine? Findings Across 63 studies, FAST reached 92.1% pooled sensitivity for hemoperitoneum, lung ultrasound 90-97% versus 60-69% for radiography; management changed in up to 44%. Critical relevance statement This review critically appraises ultraportable ultrasound across all four disaster domains, showing that radiation-free bedside imaging accelerates triage, conserves scarce CT capacity, and extends radiological expertise through tele-guidance, while exposing an evidence base still lacking prospective outcome data.

title: Large language model assistance for report-based carotid plaque AHA classification: a multi-reader study.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate whether large language model assistance improves radiologists' agreement with a text-based reference standard in inferring the modified American Heart Association carotid plaque classification from free-text MRI reports, and whether a lightweight model can perform well under criteria-guided prompting. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 433 patients from three institutions. In a report-based reader study, four radiologists classified MRI reports with and without large language model assistance. In standalone evaluation, a rule-based baseline and 10 models were compared under naive and criteria-guided prompting. The reference standard was expert consensus based on the report text. Results Among 433 patients (mean age, 65.9 years ± 13.4; 248 males), AI assistance improved six-class agreement with the text-based reference standard. At the vessel level, junior radiologists improved from 61.75% to 83.12% (Qwen3-8B) and 87.75% (DeepSeek-R1); senior radiologists from 77.00% to 87.50% and 92.25%, respectively (all Holm-corrected p < 0.001). Patient-level agreement increased from 41.0% to 78.8% (junior) and from 59.8% to 87.8% (senior) with DeepSeek-R1. Agreement increased (quadratic-weighted κ: 0.231 without AI vs 0.775 with DeepSeek-R1). In standalone evaluation, criteria-guided prompting improved Qwen3-8B agreement from 38.91% to 81.52% (95% CI: 78.87-84.06%), remaining 5.89 percentage points below DeepSeek-R1 (87.41%; 95% CI: 85.10-89.61%). Conclusion In this report-based classification setting, large language model assistance improved radiologists' agreement with the text-based reference standard, with larger gains in junior radiologists. When prompts explicitly encoded AHA criteria, an 8B local candidate model performed well, supporting its potential use as a standardization aid for text-based workflows. Key points Question Report-based modified AHA classification of carotid plaques is experience-dependent and difficult to standardize, as mapping multi-sequence imaging findings to classification conclusions imposes substantial cognitive load. Findings Large language model assistance improved agreement with a text-based reference standard and raised inter-reader consistency (weighted κ 0.231-0.775), narrowing the junior-senior gap. Critical relevance statement Embedding explicit AHA criteria in the prompt let an 8B model approach 671B-model agreement (38.91-81.52%), supporting standardized text-based workflows without fine-tuning.

title: MRI for restaging pancreatic cancer.
abstract: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is a tumor with a dismal prognosis, as the majority of patients are diagnosed when the tumor is not resectable. Neoadjuvant treatment has significantly improved prognosis, but assessing treatment response can be challenging for radiologists. Given the fibrotic nature of the primary tumor, differentiating between residual viable tumor and fibrotic response can be difficult. MRI can have a role in reassessing the primary tumor and disease spread. In this review, we discuss MR techniques that can be used for this assessment, including routinely used sequences (e.g., DWI) and sequences that are not yet routinely included in pancreatic protocols (e.g., T1 mapping, ECV imaging, and USPIO contrast for nodal staging). KEY POINTS: Question Imaging assessment of the response of pancreatic adenocarcinoma to neoadjuvant treatment is difficult and still has limited accuracy. Findings Different MRI sequences and techniques have been suggested as possibly improving this assessment, reflecting on better patient management. Critical relevance statement We summarize the available evidence on MRI for restaging pancreatic carcinoma after neoadjuvant treatment.

title: Real-time CT/MR fusion imaging-guided core needle biopsy: enhancing diagnostic precision in head and neck lesions.
abstract: Objectives To establish an intraoperative CT/MR fusion imaging (FI)-guided core needle biopsy (CNB) approach for head and neck lesions and to evaluate its diagnostic performance in comparison with conventional CT-guided biopsy. Material and methods This retrospective study included patients undergoing CT-guided or FI-guided CNB for head and neck lesions between January 2020 and December 2024. Clinical information was collected, including demographics, lesion size, needle insertion depth, number of biopsy cores obtained, and complications. Diagnostic performance was evaluated at both the case-based and core-based levels by comparing biopsy histopathology with the final diagnosis. Subgroup analyses were performed according to lesion size, needle insertion depth, and pathological type. Results A total of 152 patients with 426 biopsy cores were included, comprising 66 patients (183 cores) in the CT-guided group and 86 patients (243 cores) in the FI-guided group. At the case-based level, FI-guided biopsy demonstrated significantly higher diagnostic accuracy than CT-guided biopsy (98.8% vs 90.9%, p = 0.04), particularly for lesions < 3.7 cm and non-squamous cell carcinoma (non-SCC) lesions. At the core-based level, FI-guided biopsy also achieved higher accuracy (96.3% vs 73.2%, p < 0.001) and sensitivity (93.8% vs 65.0%, p < 0.001), with consistent advantages across all predefined subgroups. No major procedure-related complications were observed. Conclusions FI-guided CNB is a safe and feasible technique for head and neck lesions that improves diagnostic accuracy compared with conventional CT guidance. Key points Question Can CT/MR FI overcome the limitations of conventional CT guidance for precise targeting and accurate biopsy of anatomically complex head and neck lesions? Findings CT/MR FI-guided biopsy demonstrated higher diagnostic accuracy at both case-based and core-based analyses than conventional CT-guided biopsy for complex head and neck lesions. Critical relevance statement This study provides evidence that CT/MR fusion-guided biopsy improves targeting precision and diagnostic performance compared with conventional CT-guided biopsy, supporting its application for complex head and neck lesions in clinical radiology practice.

title: Estimation of glomerular filtration rate by standard renal CT imaging.
abstract: Objectives To develop and evaluate a method to predict glomerular filtration rate (GFR) from clinical renal CT. Materials and methods Medical records of adult living kidney donors operated between 2013 and 2022 and patients considered for neoadjuvant cisplatin prior to cystectomy between 2019 and 2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Inclusion criteria were (1) renal CT obtained at 100 or 120 kVp before and 5-15 min after contrast administration, and (2) iohexol clearance test within 2 months of imaging. The iohexol clearance test was performed on the same day as the cystatin C and creatinine measurements. Estimated GFR values included cystatin C-based eGFR (eGFR cystatin C ), creatinine-based eGFR using the Cockcroft-Gault formula (eGFR Cockcroft-Gault ), and eGFR using the Revised Lund-Malmö formula (eGFR LMR18 ), which is based on both creatinine and cystatin C. Manual and automatic segmentations of the renal pelvis and bladder were performed in both the excretory and unenhanced phases. Results In total, 139 patients were included in the analysis (mean age 52 ± 13 years; 60% women). Multivariate linear regression analysis combining the segmentation-derived variable with body surface area and age gave an adjusted R-square of 0.77 to mGFR iohexol (p < 0.001). GFR CT had the strongest relationship to mGFR iohexol with a mean absolute error of 12.8 mL/min, compared with 15.6 mL/min for eGFR Cockcroft-Gault , 14.2 mL/min for eGFR cystatin C , and 13.0 mL/min for eGFR LMR18 . Manual and automatic segmentations had similar performance. Patients evaluated for cisplatin treatment had greater variation in CT-estimated split renal function than donors. Conclusion Renal function can be estimated with high precision from clinical renal CT. Key points Question Accurate GFR assessment is critical, but current methods are either labor-intensive or imprecise. Can renal CT imaging provide a reliable alternative? Findings CT-derived eGFR showed the strongest correlation with iohexol clearance (R² = 0.77), with lower error compared to creatinine- and cystatin C-based estimates. Critical relevance statement Routine CT imaging can provide precise estimates of kidney function, supporting donor evaluations, chemotherapy dosing, and critical care decisions when accurate renal function is essential.

title: Probable vestibular paroxysmia mimicking benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of the superior semicircular canal in the presence of a neurovascular conflict: a case report and review of the literature.
abstract: Background Positional vertigo is a frequent complaint in otology and vestibular physiotherapy, arising from functional or structural causes affecting the peripheral or central vestibular systems. Although benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is the most common form, other etiologies such as vestibular paroxysmia (VP), central positional vertigo, or vertebrobasilar insufficiency should be considered. Recognizing the specific features and differential diagnosis of these conditions is crucial for accurate assessment. Case presentation We describe the case of a 52-year-old French woman presenting with positional vertigo initially diagnosed as a BPPV of the right superior semicircular canal. Despite multiple repositioning maneuvers, symptoms persisted. The positional downbeat and right torsional nystagmus observed in the right Dix-Hallpike test (illustrated in video) and the lack of response to treatment raised suspicion of an atypical etiology. MRI re-evaluation revealed a neurovascular conflict between the right anterior inferior cerebellar artery and the right vestibulocochlear nerve, supporting the diagnosis of probable vestibular paroxysmia mimicking a superior canal BPPV. Conclusions Positional vertigo resembling BPPV that is refractory to repositioning maneuvers or atypical should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. In particular, suspected superior canal BPPV requires heightened diagnostic caution and a comprehensive clinical assessment.

title: Multimodal imaging features of nuclear protein in testis carcinoma of the submandibular gland: a case report.
abstract: Rationale NUT carcinoma (NC) is a rare and highly aggressive malignancy defined by rearrangements of the NUTM1gene. Primary NC of the submandibular gland is exceptionally rare, with nonspecific imaging features that often lead to misdiagnosis as common salivary gland tumors and delayed treatment. Patient concerns A 32-year-old man presented with a painless mass in the left submandibular region that rapidly enlarged from 2 cm to approximately 4 cm within 1 month, accompanied by the development of ipsilateral pharyngeal and periauricular pain. Diagnoses Preoperative multimodal imaging-computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-revealed an ill-defined, invasive mass with heterogeneous enhancement and intense metabolic activity (SUVmax 18.4). The diagnosis was confirmed by histopathological examination and immunohistochemical analysis, which demonstrated diffuse nuclear positivity for NUT protein. Interventions The patient underwent radical surgical resection (left neck dissection), followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Outcomes No evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease was observed on follow-up imaging at 9 months postoperatively. Lessons This case underscores that although the imaging features of submandibular gland NC are not pathognomonic, the combination of a rapidly growing invasive mass, heterogeneous enhancement, and marked hypermetabolism should raise clinical suspicion. Prompt biopsy with NUT immunohistochemical testing is essential for definitive diagnosis and early intervention, which is critical given the tumor's highly aggressive nature.
originalAbstract:
Rationale

NUT carcinoma (NC) is a rare and highly aggressive malignancy defined by rearrangements of the NUTM1gene. Primary NC of the submandibular gland is exceptionally rare, with nonspecific imaging features that often lead to misdiagnosis as common salivary gland tumors and delayed treatment.

Patient concerns

A 32-year-old man presented with a painless mass in the left submandibular region that rapidly enlarged from 2 cm to approximately 4 cm within 1 month, accompanied by the development of ipsilateral pharyngeal and periauricular pain.

Diagnoses

Preoperative multimodal imaging-computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-revealed an ill-defined, invasive mass with heterogeneous enhancement and intense metabolic activity (SUVmax 18.4). The diagnosis was confirmed by histopathological examination and immunohistochemical analysis, which demonstrated diffuse nuclear positivity for NUT protein.

Interventions

The patient underwent radical surgical resection (left neck dissection), followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

Outcomes

No evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease was observed on follow-up imaging at 9 months postoperatively.

Lessons

This case underscores that although the imaging features of submandibular gland NC are not pathognomonic, the combination of a rapidly growing invasive mass, heterogeneous enhancement, and marked hypermetabolism should raise clinical suspicion. Prompt biopsy with NUT immunohistochemical testing is essential for definitive diagnosis and early intervention, which is critical given the tumor's highly aggressive nature.

title: Type of dialysis may influence the prognostic value of myocardial perfusion imaging in end stage renal disease: an observational [ 13 N]NH 3 PET/CT study.
abstract: Patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) exhibit an elevated risk of cardiovascular events, with imaging-based risk stratification becoming increasingly important. This study compares the prognostic utility of [13N]NH3 PET/CT assessing myocardial blood flow (MBF), coronary flow reserve (CFR) and coronary artery calcium score (CACS) as well as 3D carotid ultrasound (for carotid plaque burden; cPB) in hemodialysis (HD) versus peritoneal dialysis (PD) patients listed for kidney transplantation. 41 ESRD patients (HD n = 31; PD n = 10; median follow-up 4.9 years) without known coronary artery disease underwent myocardial perfusion imaging with [13N]NH3 PET/CT, CACS, and 3D carotid ultrasound. HD patients exhibited lower myocardial stress blood flow (MBFstress) and CFR compared to PD patients (2.67 ± 0.67 vs. 2.97 ± 0.69; p = 0.24 and 2.5 ± 0.74 vs. 3.08 ± 1.12; p = 0.07). In the HD subgroup, only MBFstress correlated inversely with CACS and cPB (r = -0.32; p < 0.05 and r = -0.44; p < 0.05), whereas CFR did not (r=-0.14; p = 0.47 and r= -0.14; p = 0.44). On the other hand, both MBFstress and CFR were predictive of cardiovascular events in HD patients, although the number of events was low (n = 4). In contrast, PD patients exhibited only one single cardiovascular event in the follow-up and no significant imaging correlations were observed. MBFstress and CFR may emerge as prognostic markers for cardiovascular events in HD patients whereas their prognostic power in PD patients remains uncertain. HD patients show more pronounced impairment in MBFstress and atherosclerotic plaque burden in the carotid artery, highlighting particularly this parameter as a prognostic marker in this group.

title: CT radiomics showed no improvement beyond volume dynamics for early lesion-level size response to immunotherapy in metastatic melanoma.
abstract: Background We evaluated whether CT intensity and texture radiomics provide predictive value beyond simple volume dynamics for lesion-level response prediction in metastatic melanoma treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. Methods We conducted a retrospective multicenter study including 158 patients (1,626 lesions) from an internal cohort (n = 129 patients with standardized protocols) and an external cohort (n = 29 patients with heterogeneous protocols). The primary endpoint was binary lesion-level size response (clinical benefit vs. progressive disease) at the second follow-up. We trained and compared Random Forest classifiers to predict this endpoint using clinical variables, volumetric features, radiomics, and combined predictors derived from baseline and first follow-up imaging. Models were trained on the internal cohort using patient-grouped cross-validation and applied unchanged to the external cohort. Paired differences in AUC were assessed against a ± 0.05 equivalence margin. Results Baseline-only prediction of first follow-up response was near chance for all models. For predicting response at second follow-up, the volumetric model achieved an internal AUC of 0.84 [95% CI 0.78-0.88] and the radiomics model 0.86 [0.81-0.90]. In the external cohort, with 12 progression events, the volumetric and radiomics models achieved AUCs of 0.68 [0.50-0.85] and 0.68 [0.51-0.88], with no significant difference between any models. Organ-specific analysis showed no significant improvement from adding radiomics for any lesion site. Across all 288 radiomic features, the median absolute correlation with lesion volume was 0.37. Sensitivity analyses contained small or borderline gains that did not replicate externally. Conclusions Volumetric features capture the primary predictive information for early lesion-level response, and CT radiomics showed no conclusive improvement over volume dynamics. Confirmation in larger independent cohorts is required before radiomic signatures can be recommended for this task. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: ACR lung-RADS: updates and future directions.
abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and low-dose CT (LDCT) screening has been shown to significantly reduce lung cancer deaths in high-risk populations. The American College of Radiology (ACR) introduced the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS) in 2014 to standardize the reporting and management of screen-detected pulmonary nodules. Since its inception, Lung-RADS has undergone iterative updates reflecting advances in evidence, clinical practice, and the expanding scope of lung cancer screening. This review summarizes the major updates to Lung-RADS, highlights areas of active discussion within the Lung-RADS Committee, and outlines future research directions. Key topics include the ongoing evaluation of volumetric versus diameter-based nodule measurement, the management of subsolid nodules and the balance between surveillance and intervention, the implementation of Category 0 for infectious or inflammatory findings, clarification of juxtapleural nodule classification, the approach to incidental findings, and the development of a Lung-RADS Atlas. Future directions address the integration of risk-based and category-based assessment approaches, the role of artificial intelligence and deep learning in nodule stratification, the potential incorporation of incidental nodules into Lung-RADS, and the prospect of international harmonization for lung cancer screening reporting and management. Lung-RADS has become an essential reporting and quality tool for lung cancer screening in the United States and increasingly worldwide. Continued refinement, guided by emerging evidence, multidisciplinary collaboration, and technological innovation, will be critical to advancing precision screening strategies and reducing the global burden of lung cancer.Clinical trial numberNot applicable.

title: Bridging radiomics and histopathology: cross-modality consistency of radiomic features from CT to micro-CT in NSCLC.
abstract: Objective Radiomics extracts quantitative features from medical images that may provide non-invasive biomarkers of tumor biology and heterogeneity. However, few studies have explored radiomics on micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) or its transferability to clinical CT. This study investigates the reproducibility and the potential biological correlation of radiomic features across in vivo CT, ex vivo CT, and ex vivo micro-CT in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Materials and methods A retrospective cohort of 60 NSCLC patients with preoperative CT scans and surgical specimens was analyzed. Ex vivo CT and micro-CT images were acquired and compared with in vivo CT using standardized preprocessing, including normalization, resampling, and registration. Tumor regions of interest (ROIs) were semi-automatically segmented, and 93 radiomic features were extracted with Pyradiomics. Cross-modality reproducibility and associations with histotype were evaluated using Spearman correlation, intraclass correlation coefficient, Bland-Altman analysis, and Mann-Whitney U test. Results Normalization and volume matching improved feature repeatability, with the highest agreement observed in normalized datasets using subsampled ROIs. Four texture-based features consistently showed high reproducibility and potential biological correlation, likely reflecting intratumoral heterogeneity and variation in cell density: DependenceNonUniformity, GrayLevelNonUniformity (GLDM and GLRLM), and Coarseness (NGTDM). These features reliably distinguished adenocarcinoma from squamous cell carcinoma across modalities, confirming their stability and potential as candidate features for transferable biomarkers. Conclusion Harmonization and volume standardization are essential for cross-modality radiomic analyses. Stable texture features provide a potential transferable signature bridging micro-CT and clinical CT imaging in NSCLC, supporting their role as candidate features for further investigation in biologically oriented studies. Key points Question Micro-CT serves as an intermediate imaging scale enabling radiomic feature extraction from ex vivo NSCLC tumors, allowing direct comparison with in vivo and ex vivo CT. Findings Intensity normalization and volume-matched subsampling between in vivo CT, ex vivo CT, and micro-CT reduced cross-modality feature variability, improving feature reproducibility. Relevance statement Normalization, volume matching, and cross-modality analysis support the identification of candidate texture features with consistent cross-scale behavior and exploratory associations with NSCLC histotype.

title: Radiomics machine learning models for lung cancer early diagnosis in heterogenous multicentre chest CT data: LIBRA study results.
abstract: Objective We developed and validated radiomics models for lung cancer prediction in indeterminate pulmonary nodules that retain performance in heterogenous data from multiple centres. Materials and methods The retrospective Lung Imaging Biobank for Radiomics and AI (LIBRA) study recruited 1,026 patients (2,071 computed tomography scans) with 5-to-30-mm lung nodules from seven UK hospitals (01/07/2020-30/09/2022). Benign and malignant nodules were segmented for feature extraction using PyRadiomics. Principal component analysis reduced feature dimensionality to twenty components. Logistic regression models using ComBat correction, fixed effects or random effects to mitigate for disparate data across study centres were compared. Models were fit to the whole dataset and evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. Internal-external validation assessed between-centre heterogeneity. Models were benchmarked against volume, Brock score and scrambled voxels. Calibration was assessed using calibration curves. Decision-curve analysis was used to assess net benefit. Results Between-centre discrimination variability was observed with an area under the curve (AUC) ranging 0.75-0.91. The mixed-effects model provided better discrimination over ComBat or fixed effects alone (AUC 0.91 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.90-0.93) versus 0.75 (95% CI: 0.72-0.78) and 0.88 (95% CI: 0.86-0.90), respectively (p < 0.0001 and 0.003, respectively) in cross-validation. Radiomics features retained significance in multivariable models including established clinical features. The final model was superior to models developed using volume alone, Brock score, and scrambled-voxels. The model was well calibrated (intercept -0.036, slope 0.89 with net benefit compared to volume or Brock score alone. Conclusion Radiomics models show between-centre heterogeneity, with resilience best achieved with mixed-effects models. The final model had high performance with net benefit over established risk models. Key points Question Can heterogeneous data from multiple centres be used to predict lung nodule malignancy risk? Findings Radiomics cancer prediction models must account for heterogeneity to maintain performance between different centres. The mixed-effects model achieved AUC 0.91 (cross-validation) for cancer prediction. Relevance statement The model provided net benefit for nodule investigation over Brock score and volume alone and could assist in decision-making following prospective validation.

title: Fully automated diaphragm segmentation on routine 2D-cine and 3D thoracic MRI: multireader validation.
abstract: Objective The diaphragm is central to respiratory mechanics and may be impaired in various diseases. Parametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment is limited by time-consuming manual segmentation. We developed and validated fully automated diaphragm segmentation on two-dimensional (2D)-cine and three-dimensional (3D) thoracic MRI. Materials and methods In this single-center study, eligible adults without known diaphragmatic disorders underwent 2D-cine MRI, 3D MRI, or both. Two U-Net models (2D/3D) were trained using expert manual contours as ground truth. title: Phase-adaptive automated whole-liver quantification of signal intensity-derived liver indices from gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI.
abstract: Objectives To develop and validate a phase-adaptive pipeline for automated whole-liver, parenchyma-based quantification of signal intensity-derived liver indices from gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI without inter-phase co-registration. Materials and methods In this retrospective, single-center study (2016-2025), 9,013 liver MRI examinations were screened, and 3,112 gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI examinations were identified. The first examination per patient defined the clinical cohort (1,174 patients; mean age, 59.6 ± 14 years [range, 4-93 years]; 611 men). A phase-adaptive nnU-Net was trained on 403 and tested on 500 dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI sequences for segmentation of liver parenchyma, intrahepatic non-parenchymal structures, and spleen; paraspinal muscle reference regions were obtained using TotalSegmentator. Segmentation accuracy was assessed against manually corrected reference segmentations generated by a semi-automatic annotation workflow with Dice similarity coefficients. Automated arterial enhancement fraction (AEF), relative liver enhancement (RLE), hepatocellular uptake index (HUI), liver-to-spleen ratio (LSR), and liver-to-muscle ratio (LMR) were compared with manual region-of-interest measurements in a radiological validation cohort (50 patients) using intraclass correlation coefficients and Bland-Altman analysis. Liver indices were compared between patients with cirrhotic and non-cirrhotic livers using the Mann-Whitney U-test. Results Liver parenchyma segmentation achieved Dice similarity coefficients of 0.998-0.999. Reader-model agreement for the liver indices ranged from 0.936 to 0.977. HUI, LSR, RLE, and LMR were lower in cirrhosis (p < 0.001), whereas AEF did not differ (p = 0.14). Conclusion Phase-adaptive segmentation enables whole-liver quantification of signal intensity-derived liver indices without inter-phase co-registration. The lower hepatobiliary uptake indices in cirrhosis support the plausibility of this approach for scalable quantitative assessment of liver MRI. Key points Question Can gadoxetic acid-enhanced liver MRI be quantified automatically across contrast phases without inter-phase co-registration or manual region-of-interest placement in routine clinical imaging? Findings Phase-adaptive segmentation enabled automated whole-liver quantification with liver Dice coefficients of 0.998-0.999 and excellent agreement with manual measurements for five liver indices. Relevance Statement Automated whole-liver quantification from standard gadoxetic acid-enhanced liver MRI provides reproducible, signal-intensity-derived liver indices and reduces dependence on manual region-of-interest measurements in large-scale clinical studies.

title: CT-based multi-station lymph-node radiomics for preoperative prediction of lymph node metastasis in colorectal cancer: a proof-of-concept comparison with primary-tumor radiomics.
abstract: Objective Accurate preoperative prediction of lymph node metastasis (LNM) in colorectal cancer remains challenging using conventional CT assessment. This proof-of-concept study compared CT-based multi-station lymph-node radiomics with primary-tumor radiomics for patient-level preoperative prediction of LNM. Materials and methods This single-center retrospective study included patients with pathologically confirmed colorectal cancer who underwent preoperative contrast-enhanced CT and surgical resection. Patients were divided into training and validation cohorts. Radiomics features were extracted from the primary tumor and visible regional lymph nodes across multiple nodal stations. Three radiomics strategies were developed and compared: primary-tumor radiomics, multi-station lymph-node radiomics, and combined radiomics. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration analysis, decision curve analysis, and five-fold cross-validation. Pairwise AUCs were compared using the DeLong test. A clinical-radiomic model was further constructed by integrating the optimal radiomics strategy with preoperative clinical variables. Results In the validation cohort, the multi-station lymph-node radiomics model outperformed the primary-tumor radiomics model for predicting LNM (AUC, 0.864 versus 0.637; p = 0.0055). The combined radiomics model achieved an AUC of 0.840, without significant improvement over the lymph-node model (p = 0.2211). After integration with clinical variables, the clinical-radiomic model achieved an AUC of 0.879. Conclusion CT-based multi-station lymph-node radiomics showed significantly higher validation performance than primary-tumor radiomics for patient-level preoperative LNM prediction in colorectal cancer. However, this single-center proof-of-concept model is not ready for direct clinical implementation and requires multicenter external validation before clinical translation. Key points Question Can CT-based multi-station lymph-node radiomics improve preoperative nodal metastasis prediction beyond primary-tumor radiomics in patients with surgically treated colorectal cancer? Findings Multi-station lymph-node radiomics achieved higher validation performance than primary-tumor radiomics for patient-level prediction of pathological lymph-node metastasis in colorectal cancer. Relevance statement CT-based multi-station lymph-node radiomics may support individualized preoperative nodal risk stratification in colorectal cancer, but multicenter validation and prospective evaluation are required before clinical translation.

title: Preoperative prediction of HCC microvascular invasion by multimodel peritumoral diffusion MRI.
abstract: Objective Most studies emphasize intratumoral diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) metrics, but few studies have examined whether peritumoral DWI metrics can provide added value. We aimed to evaluate three-dimensional, multiscale, multimodel DWI parameters within intratumoral and peritumoral volumes of interest for predicting microvascular invasion (MVI) in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Materials and methods Seventy patients with HCC, including 42 with MVI, were prospectively enrolled. We calculated parameters from monoexponential, intravoxel incoherent motion, diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), stretched-exponential model (SEM), and continuous-time random-walk models within the tumor and in 3-mm (P3) and 5-mm (P5) peritumoral rims. Features showing differences on univariable analysis were further screened using logistic regression with variance inflation factor filtering to build combined models. Diagnostic performance was assessed by areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Results Four intratumoral diffusion-coefficient-related metrics showed significant differences between groups. In the peritumoral regions, 12 parameters differed between groups, including diffusion-coefficient-related indices and heterogeneity-related metrics. Among single parameters, P3_DKI_K app achieved the best discrimination for MVI (AUROC = 0.713); P5_DKI_K app and Tumor_SEM_DDC were selected as independent imaging predictors. After integrating alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and tumor size, the combined model (Cli-IntraPeriDWI) yielded the best performance (AUROC = 0.844). SHAP analysis indicated that higher AFP, larger tumor size, higher P5_DKI_K app , and lower Tumor_SEM_DDC were associated with increased MVI risk. Conclusion Peritumoral DWI offers multiple biomarkers and outperforms intratumoral metrics for MVI prediction. An interpretable model integrating peritumoral and intratumoral DWI with clinical factors enables accurate, noninvasive preoperative MVI risk stratification in HCC. Key points Question Can multiscale, multimodel peritumoral DWI metrics improve preoperative prediction of MVI in HCC compared with intratumoral DWI metrics? Findings Compared with intratumoral DWI, peritumoral DWI offered more potential imaging biomarkers and superior diagnostic capability for the preoperative diagnosis of MVI in HCC. Relevance statement By integrating intratumoral and peritumoral metrics with clinical risk factors, we developed a model achieving optimal performance and transparent decision interpretability for MVI assessment, supporting preoperative prognostic evaluation and individualized treatment planning in HCC.

title: Automated thigh muscle segmentation using foundation models: validation and impact of segmentation quality.
abstract: Objectives This study aimed to validate a segmentation pipeline for the extraction of volumetric thigh muscle data, investigate the influence of demographics on segmentation performance, and investigate the influence of low-quality segmentations on quantitative performance and downstream metrics. Materials and methods Manual thigh muscle segmentations on axial T1-weighted spin echo thigh images of 364 (106 training and validation; 258 testing) participants of the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) were used. A trained YOLO (You Only Look Once) object detection model generated labels and box predictions, that were passed to a fine-tuned foundation model (Segment Anything, Meta), which generated muscle segmentations. The quality of segmentations was assessed by two radiologists (none, minor, major issue), and Dice scores and mean bias versus manual segmentations were calculated in the testing dataset. Linear regression was used to calculate the associations of age, sex, and BMI with Dice scores. Results Dice scores ranged between 0.97 (quadriceps) and 0.89 (adductors). Exclusion of erroneous segmentations decreased mean bias by 0.06 mL across muscle groups; mean Dice of segmentations with versus without major issues was 0.90 versus 0.94. Female sex was associated with marginally lower Dice scores (beta -0.01, 95% CI: -0.02, -0.01, p < 0.001), while no other demographic feature showed significant associations. Conclusion Foundation models can be fine-tuned on a modest task-specific dataset to achieve segmentation accuracy comparable to bespoke networks, without training a dedicated architecture from scratch. Visually erroneous segmentations introduce only negligible degradation of quantitative performance and downstream metrics and may thus be challenging to identify by data-driven detection strategies. Key points Question Foundation models can be efficiently leveraged for robust segmentation on complex thigh muscle anatomy Findings Radiologist-identified erroneous segmentations introduced only negligible degradation of summary quantitative performance and are thus difficult to identify using statistical methods. Relevance statement Human-in-the-loop quality assurance post-validation adds limited value to improve downstream volumetric muscle metrics in foundation-model-based thigh segmentation. These findings carry implications for both research and potential clinical applications of muscle volume quantification, e.g., personalized therapeutic regimens.

title: Beyond radiotheranostics: how imaging modality defines theranostics.
abstract: Theranostics integrates diagnostic imaging and therapy within a single platform, enabling image-guided treatment delivery, real-time monitoring, and therapeutic optimization. The choice of imaging modality fundamentally shapes the design, functionality, and clinical maturity of theranostic systems. This review examines the theranostic concept through the lens of major imaging modalities employed in clinical and preclinical practice, including positron emission tomography (PET), single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), ultrasound (US), optical imaging (OI), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and computed tomography (CT). Beyond modality-specific approaches, the review highlights emerging multimodal theranostic strategies that integrate complementary imaging technologies to overcome individual limitations, enhance biological specificity, and improve treatment guidance. For each modality, we discuss the structural components of theranostic agents, their mechanisms of action, and the balance between diagnostic sensitivity and therapeutic efficacy. The review also highlights current and emerging clinical applications across major disease areas, while critically addressing limitations, such as spatial resolution, depth penetration, toxicity, and translational barriers. Overall, this article underscores that theranostics are expanding from modality-defined implementation toward integrated, multimodal strategies that are likely to shape the next generation of personalized and precision imaging-guided therapies. RELEVANCE STATEMENT : Imaging modality-driven theranostic design enables more precise, adaptive, and personalized image-guided therapies by aligning diagnostic sensitivity with therapeutic mechanisms, thereby improving treatment selection, response monitoring, and translational integration across clinical disciplines. KEY POINTS: Theranostics is determined by the underlying imaging modality rather than by a unified theranostic framework. Imaging modality dictates integration strategy. Nuclear medicine theranostics are clinically established, while MRI-, CT-, ultrasound-, and optical-based theranostics remain largely translational or function primarily as image-guided therapies. Multimodal theranostics address modality-specific limitations. Future progress depends on imaging-driven design and standardization.

title: Evaluation of iodine detection and quantification limits in photon-counting CT-a phantom study.
abstract: Objective Clinical decisions using CT iodine maps are based on evaluation of contrast enhancement, making it essential to understand how accurately CT systems detect and quantify iodine, yet quantitative evaluations remain scarce, and few studies treat iodine as an analyte for which detection threshold, quantification precision, and measurement linearity can be determined using standard laboratory-science concepts. No study has applied such concepts across photon-counting CT (PCCT) and dual-energy CT (DECT) systems. Materials and methods Using head and abdominal protocols, test tubes with iodine concentrations (0.0-2.0 mg/mL) were placed in a phantom providing head- and abdomen-equivalent attenuation. Scans were performed at two dose levels per protocol, on two DECT and one PCCT system. Iodine images were reconstructed for repeated scans using varying iterative reconstruction (IR) levels. Limit-of-detection (LoD), limit-of-quantification (LoQ), and lower-limit-of-linear-interval (LLLI) were calculated for two ROI sizes (3 and 10 mm), and differences between scanners were analyzed with Welch ANOVA and Games-Howell tests (α = 0.05). Results PCCT demonstrated significantly lower LoD/LoQ values than the DECT systems across most protocols. For low-dose abdomen (3 mGy, medium-IR), LoD for 3 and 10 mm ROI size were 0.78 and 0.16 mg/mL (PCCT), 1.28 and 0.26 mg/mL (split-filter CT), and 1.42 and 0.57 mg/mL (dual-source CT). LoQ values were also lower for PCCT. Improvements were most pronounced in low-dose protocols, with LoD reductions up to 68% (brain) and 45% (abdomen). LLLI was similar across systems. Conclusion PCCT outperformed DECT in iodine detection and quantification, particularly in low-dose protocols. These findings highlight the potential use of reduced iodine contrast and/or radiation dose. Key points Question Objective comparison of iodine detection and quantification performance between PCCT and DECT systems remains limited, particularly for low-iodine contrast media doses. Findings PCCT achieved significantly lower detection and quantification thresholds than conventional CT systems, particularly for small lesions and low-dose imaging protocols. Relevance statement Task-based LoD and LoQ metrics enable objective comparison of CT system performance and may provide clinically relevant thresholds for iodine detectability, quantification, and protocol optimization.

title: Fluent but not fail-safe: machine-translated radiology reports still need expert review.
abstract: Objectives Cross-border care, teleradiology, and international referral pathways increasingly require radiology report translation, but isolated mistranslations may alter clinical meaning. We evaluated German-to-English machine translation of radiology reports and correction-based localization of text requiring review. Materials and methods In this retrospective study, 310 de-identified German radiology reports from June and July 2025 were translated into English with DeepL. Eight radiologists assigned 5-point quality scores and corrected perceived errors. Thirty reports were reviewed by all eight readers, and 280 reports were assigned for single-reader evaluation, yielding 520 evaluations. Automated metrics and large language model judges were tested for report-level identification of translations requiring review; a correction-based segment-level edit-prediction model was evaluated on held-out shared reports. Results Most translations were rated good or excellent (339/520, 65.2%), but clinically important mistranslations involved diagnosis, anatomy, and radiologic terminology. Agreement was low for ordinal quality scores (Krippendorff α = 0.078, p = 0.006) but high for expert corrections (pairwise "bilingual evaluation understudy"-BLEU = 83.0, p < 0.001). In the conservative primary screen of 30 shared reports, no automated method discriminated translations requiring review (area under receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] = 0.51-0.65; p = 0.100-0.920). The final edit-prediction model achieved a concordance index of 0.697 and an AUC of 0.731 for segments edited by at least six of eight readers. Conclusion Machine-translated radiology reports were often acceptable on average, but translations containing errors requiring expert review persisted. Expert corrections were more reproducible than ordinal quality scores and supported localization of text requiring human review. Key points Question Cross-border radiology workflows increasingly require report translation, but fluent machine translations may still contain meaning-changing errors requiring expert review for safe care. Findings Most machine translations were rated good or excellent, yet clinically important mistranslations occurred, and automated report-level metrics did not reliably identify reports needing review. Relevance statement Machine translation may support cross-border radiology workflows, but clinically important mistranslations in otherwise fluent reports require human-in-the-loop oversight and tools that localize text requiring expert review.

title: Infected von Meyenburg complex causing recurrent gram‑negative septicaemia: the critical diagnostic role of FDG‑PET/CT in a patient with hidradenitis suppurativa.
abstract: Background von Meyenburg complex (VMC) is a rare ductal plate malformation, typically presenting as asymptomatic benign intrahepatic biliary microhamartomas. However, when secondarily infected, VMC can become the source of cryptic recurrent septicaemia, posing a substantial diagnostic challenge, particularly in patients with a known history of chronic source of comorbid infection. Case presentation A 73-year-old man with long-standing hidradenitis suppurativa presented with over ten episodes of recurrent gram-negative septicaemia. Extensive conventional imaging, including a 67 Gallium scintigraphy in another hospital, failed to identify an infectious source. Due to persistent diagnostic uncertainty, ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT was performed. The scan revealed an enlarged liver with heterogeneously increased ¹⁸F-FDG uptake exhibiting an "inverted pyramidal" metabolic configuration: a wide base of activity along the subcapsular dome of superior hepatic segments converged centripetally towards the porta hepatis, thereby casting a tree-like three-dimensional anatomy of the biliary radicles. CT findings were non-specific, showing vaguely scattered mixed densities, greatly outnumbered by the hypermetabolic foci. Constellation of these findings suggests a non-dilated ductal infectious process, leading to the presumptive diagnosis of infected VMC with micro-abscesses. Subsequent MRI/MRCP confirmed numerous tiny T2‑weighted bright signals of varying sizes and intensities in agreement with the "starry sky" pattern of biliary hamartomas. Targeted levofloxacin therapy based on susceptibility testing resulted in resolution of fever and septic parameters. A follow-up ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT scan three weeks after treatment demonstrated complete metabolic quiescence and resolution of previously documented intrahepatic hypermetabolic foci. Conclusion ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT has proven value in investigation for fever of unknown origin. This case illustrates the value of this imaging not only in precise localization of the infectious source but also provides a suggestive metabolic pattern leading to the diagnosis of a rare congenital biliary condition, VMC, as a hidden source of infection otherwise masked by other comorbid infectious foci. Revealing the true source of loculated infection and its mechanism of spread leads to appropriate antibiotic therapy and treatment monitoring.

title: Detection rate of PSMA PET MRI (18 F-Flotufolastat) at the onset of biochemical recurrence following radical prostatectomy.
abstract: Purpose The optimal timing to obtain the initial PET-PSMA imaging study when disease recurrence is suspected following RP is controversial. Methods 24 subjects with new onset of BCR following RP were enrolled. The initial PET MRI (study #1) was performed within 2 months of signing informed consent. Salvage treatment was offered only if site(s) of disease recurrence were identified by study #1. A second PSMA PET MRI (study #2) was performed 1 year following Study 1, or sooner if the 6-month PSA was > 0.5 ng/ml. PET/MR was performed in a dedicated scanner which allows simultaneous acquisition of PET and MR images following the IV administration of 8 m Ci of 18 F-Flotufolastat (18F-rH PSMA, Blue Earth Diagnostics, UK). Results Disease recurrence was identified in 25% and 40% of subjects by study #1 and study #2, respectively. PSA doubling time with and without disease recurrence on study #2 was 12.8 months (IQR 4.0-17.2) and 20.8 months (20.8 months (IQR 9.1-51.7), respectively (p = 0.27). PSA prior to RP but not age, pathological grade, stage margin status or time to recurrence were significantly different between subjects with and without localization of disease recurrence. Conclusions The 25% disease detection and localizations justify performing PSMA PET MRI imaging at the onset of BCR. If the initial PSMA PET MRI does not identify site(s) of disease, our study supports repeating a PSMA PET study when the PSA is > 0.5 ng/ml or if the PSA doubling time is < 1 year. Clinical trial record The study is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with study number NCT05678322.- Registration date 12/28/2022 URL of trial registry record: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05678322.

title: Expanding role of nuclear medicine in cardiac amyloidosis: insights from the EJNMMI collection.
abstract: Recent advances in nuclear medicine are reshaping the evaluation of cardiac amyloidosis, as highlighted by the recent collection published in EJNMMI (collection link: https://link.springer.com/collections/igfdhcddjg). This commentary summarizes key insights from these studies, emphasizing the evolving shift from conventional diagnostic imaging toward a more integrated and comprehensive approach. Emerging developments include novel amyloid PET tracers, improved diagnostic accuracy with SPECT/CT, multimodality imaging strategies, and enhanced assessment of systemic disease burden extending beyond the left ventricle. There is also growing interest in longitudinal monitoring, pre-symptomatic detection, and the role of artificial intelligence. Together, these advances position nuclear medicine as an essential tool for disease characterization, risk stratification, and treatment assessment.

title: Effect of data-driven gating on the quantification of prostate cancer metastases in <sup>68</sup>Ga-PSMA- and ¹⁸F-DCFPyL-PSMA PET/CT.
abstract: Background PSMA PET/CT using 18 F‑DCFPyL and 68 Ga‑labelled tracers is central to prostate cancer staging, but 68 Ga‑PSMA may show reduced sensitivity and quantitative accuracy, partly due to respiratory motion and lower spatial resolution. Device-based motion‑correction methods have limitations. Data‑driven gating (DDG) offers a hardware‑free alternative, though its impact on PSMA PET, especially 68 Ga‑PSMA has not been systematically evaluated. To evaluate the quantitative and qualitative performance of the DDG motion-correction method in 68 Ga-PSMA and 18 F-DCFPyL-PSMA PET/CT, focusing on metastatic lymph node, lung, and bone lesions, and to assess its robustness across tracers. Methods This retrospective study included patients with biopsy‑proven prostate cancer who underwent 68 Ga‑PSMA or 18 F‑DCFPyL PSMA PET/CT for primary staging or biochemical recurrence and had metastatic disease. Motion correction was applied using the OncoFreeze AI™ data‑driven gating (OFAI‑DDG) method. Metastatic lesions were segmented semi‑automatically, and SUV metrics, image noise, and contrast‑to‑noise ratio were quantified by anatomical site in both OFAI-DDG and static images. Qualitative image quality was independently scored by two experienced readers. Statistical analyses included non‑parametric tests, Bland-Altman agreement, regression analyses, tracer comparison, and inter‑reader reliability assessment. Results After exclusions, 23 68 Ga‑PSMA and 40 18 F‑PSMA patients were analyzed, yielding 133 and 192 metastatic lesions, respectively. OFAI‑DDG reconstruction significantly increased SUV mean and SUV max compared with static imaging for both tracers across bone, lymph node, and lung lesions (p < 0.0001), with the largest gains in lung lesions. CNR improved for most lesion types, and image noise was significantly reduced. Qualitative analysis showed better image quality, sharpness, and noise with OFAI‑DDG, with high inter‑reader agreement. OFAI‑DDG performance was robust across tracers and largely independent of lesion location. Conclusions This study demonstrates that OFAI‑DDG significantly improves PSMA PET/CT image quality and quantitative accuracy compared with standard static imaging. The improvements were observed for both 68 Ga‑PSMA and 18 F‑PSMA tracers, indicating tracer‑independent robustness. The OFAI‑DDG simplified the workflow and reduced time used for patient set-up, while enhancing lesion visualization and quantitative reliability without altering lesion detection, supporting its clinical value for metastatic prostate cancer imaging.

title: Post-embolization dynamic changes in Obsidio Conformable Embolic: volume and radiodensity analysis.
abstract: To characterize the temporal dynamic and clinical remodeling of the Obsidio™ Conformable Embolic (Obsidio) post endovascular delivery using longitudinal quantitative CT volumetry and Hounsfield unit (HU) attenuation. This retrospective, single-center cohort study included 21 patients (30 vessels) embolized with Obsidio for acute hemorrhage or hypervascular tumor between 2023 and 2026. Patients had at least two follow-up computed tomography (CT) scans. The primary endpoint was the percent change in embolic cast volume and HU attenuation, measured using standardized Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) segmentation tools. Secondary endpoints included assessment for recanalization. All embolizations were technically successful (100%). On the first follow-up CT (median 12 days), the mean Obsidio volume was 89.33 ± 13.86% of the original volume (p = 0.0002). On the second follow-up (median 36 days), the volume was 79.51 ± 19.76% of baseline volume (p = 0.0004), representing 20.49% reduction. On third follow-up CT (median 76 days), volume was 85.2 ± 18.92% (p = 0.047). On the fourth follow-up CT, volume was 66.76 ± 16.9% (p = 0.0048). On the fifth follow-up CT, volume was 60.15 ± 3.15% (p = 0.00001) The average volume reduction rate decelerated from 0.99%/day to 0.71%/day to 0.17%/day then stabilized at 0.2%/day. Concurrently, mean Hounsfield unit attenuation increased by 4.85% (p = 0.06) on the second follow-up CT scan. No evidence of recanalization, distal embolization, or cast fragmentation was observed on any of CT scans. The Obsidio embolic cast undergoes progressive reduction in volume and increase in HU attenuation over time without evidence of vessel recanalization. This temporal dynamic of Obsidio embolic is consistent with bioresorption of its gelatin and water components, supporting the concept of persistent occlusion via in vivo remodeling.

title: Stroke-associated pneumonia: from immunodepression to bedside management and future research directions.
abstract: Stroke-associated pneumonia (SAP) is one of the most frequent complications after acute stroke, affecting approximately one in eight stroke patients. Besides prolonged hospitalisation and increased healthcare costs, it is also a major risk factor for mortality and poor functional recovery. The pathophysiology of SAP is driven by two converging processes: impaired local airway defence due to dysphagia as well as reduced airway clearance reflexes, and systemic stroke-induced immunodepression driven by dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system. While post-stroke immunodepression is a major risk factor for SAP, it might limit unwanted autoimmune responses within the brain. Conversely, SAP itself may drive neuroinflammation and contribute to post-stroke cognitive impairment. Despite its clinical importance, high-quality evidence to guide practice on prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of SAP remains scarce and guideline recommendations are mostly based on expert consensus. Diagnosis of SAP is suggested to be based on standardised clinical criteria supported by chest radiography and C-reactive protein as an adjunct where uncertainty persists. After diagnosis, guidelines suggest prompt empirical antibiotic therapy according to local protocols. In contrast, preventive antibiotics, even for high-risk patients, neither improve clinical outcome nor reduce SAP frequency. Currently recommended preventive strategies for SAP therefore mostly focus on dysphagia management and early mobilisation. This review integrates the pathophysiology, long-term consequences of SAP and further research directions based on the current knowledge on post-stroke immunology with prevention, diagnosis and treatment of SAP as set out in the recent European Stroke Organisation guideline and related guidelines.
